turns.prompt_text: Here is the comprehensive architectural summary of your Evolutionary Modular Dimensional TDD system, structured so another agent can instantly ingest the context, mechanics, and philosophy of the project. System Overview: Agentic Liquid Software This system is an automated engine designed not just to write software, but to perform epistemological research. It treats code as "liquid software" that hardens into a crystallized state. The ultimate goal is to find an optimal solution, simplify it under arbitrary constraints, and extract the underlying theoretical "root" to build a multidimensional ontology of problem spaces. The Team Hierarchy Project Manager: Handles the highest-level Specification Contract (out of scope for this summary). Team Lead (The Core State Machine): Manages resources, enforces progression, evaluates success, and dictates mitigation or compression strategies. Workers (Documenter, Tester, Programmer, Architect): Specialized agents that execute localized tasks within strictly bounded contexts. Core Mechanics 1. The Single-Wheel Sequential Turn-Taking To avoid Git merge conflicts and asynchronous state corruption, the system operates on a single, deterministic thread. The Prediction: The Team Lead reads the spec, provisions a budget of agentic credits, and creates a predictive Roadmap. The Handoff: The Team Lead selects one worker, provisions its context, and yields the "wheel." The Execution & Return: The worker mutates the workspace, logs its actions, and immediately returns the wheel to the Team Lead. The Delta: The Team Lead compares the actual workspace reality against its initial prediction to inform its next move. 2. File-System as Database (State Management) Task progression is tracked entirely through the file system to prevent worker myopia and enforce permission boundaries. Structure: /milestones/01_core_logic/task_01... state.yaml (Team Lead writes, Worker reads): Contains the localized specification, objectives, and status (pending, complete). worker_log.md (Worker writes, Team Lead reads): The worker provides a "proof of work" and justification mapping its actions to the YAML requirements. test_results.json (Automated): Provides the objective ground truth. Workflow: A task is only marked complete by the Team Lead when tests are green and the worker's logic aligns. Completed tasks are managed via directory renaming (e.g., prepending done_). The Development Pipeline 1. Strict Linear Progression The methodology mandates that phases cannot begin until the predecessor is complete: Specification Contract ➔ Documentation (High to Low) ➔ Testing (BDD/TDD) ➔ Programming Note: Testing and Programming are highly coupled, but tests must drive the code. 2. Failure as a Feature If a specification fails to harden into code, the Team Lead does not infinitely debug. It uses the remaining budget to query workers, compile a Retrospective Artifact, and push accountability back up to the Project Manager to fix the foundational specification. Technical Debt & Complexity Management Technical debt is quantified as Context Friction—the cognitive load that causes agents to hallucinate or burn excessive tokens. 1. The Debt Multiplier At each checkpoint, a local script analyzes the codebase to calculate a multiplier based on: AST Node Density: Overall volume of logic. Cyclomatic Complexity: Nested logic and branching paths. Dependency Fan-Out: Number of external imports/modules. Struggle Coefficient: How many back-and-forth turns were required to complete the task. 2. The Feasibility Check & Compression Phase Before allocating credits for the next milestone, the Team Lead runs: Credits Remaining > (Base Task Cost * Debt Multiplier) If this fails, the system triggers the Compression Phase: The Team Lead halts forward progress. An Architect agent is provisioned. The Team Lead applies arbitrary constraints (e.g., "no nested loops") and tasks the Architect with reducing the Debt Multiplier while keeping test_results.json 100% green. This forces the system out of localized maximums, stripping away human-like procedural complexity to find the mathematical or theoretical root solution. The Ontology & Metadata Index The final output of this system is a linked knowledge graph mapping the abstract problem space. When a Compression Phase successfully uncovers a theoretical "Root" solution, the Team Lead documents it in a highly structured Markdown file: YAML Frontmatter: Contains machine-readable metrics (domain, debt multiplier, constraints applied) that are scraped by a decoupled metadata index. This allows the Team Lead to programmatically query past solutions before beginning new runs. Bidirectional Wiki-Links: Connects the Root node Up:: to the abstract problem, Origin:: to the failed state that spawned it, and Validated_By:: to its test suite. Narrative Abstraction: The markdown body explains the theoretical paradigm discovered (e.g., "This problem is matrix transformation, not sequential validation"), serving as a perfect prompt injection for future agentic context windows. -------- Architecture Specification: Evolutionary Modular Dimensional TDD Framework This document outlines the design, mechanics, and philosophy of a multi-agent automated software development pipeline. It is designed to be ingested by a clean-context agent to continue development or implementation of the framework. Core Philosophy: Spec-Driven Evolution This framework rejects the sunk-cost fallacy of infinitely debugging broken code. The Specification Contract (managed as a linked Markdown graph) is the immutable source of truth. The resulting code is a disposable iteration. If the code fails to compile or pass tests, the system assumes the specification was ambiguous or logically flawed. The pipeline is designed to fail fast, extract the exact point of friction, kill the execution environment, and use that failure data to mutate the specification. You do not fix the code; you harden the spec and try again. Agent Hierarchy & Roles 1. The Project Manager (Strategic Layer) Role: The architect, resource economist, and graph owner. Responsibilities: Manages the overarching system specification as a local-first, linked Markdown graph topology. Provisions new Team Leads with a specific Markdown node (work package) and an initial budget of Agentic Credits. Ingests failure data to isolate faults in the graph and executes surgical mutations on the spec before relaunching the pipeline. 2. The Team Lead (State Machine / Managerial Layer) Role: The tactical execution controller and state evaluator. Responsibilities: Enforces strict pipeline progression: Specification -> Documentation -> Testing -> Programming. Progression cannot happen out of order. Manages a maximum of 4 active worker sessions, keeping role contexts strictly bounded to prevent overlap. Allocates "micro-budgets" of credits to workers per turn. Calculates the "Delta" between predicted workflow health and actual worker outputs. Triggers the "Kill Switch" (Guillotine) if the Delta exceeds recoverable thresholds, compiling a Retrospective Artifact for the Project Manager. 3. The Workers (Execution Layer) Role: Specialized, single-purpose agents (Documenter, Tester, Programmer). Responsibilities: Execute specific tasks within a rigid micro-budget. The Tester: Acts as a literal translator. Translates Markdown directly into automated tests. Must use DocRefs for strict traceability. Forbidden from hallucinating missing constraints; treats ambiguity as a fatal blocker. The Programmer: Acts as a constraint-solver. Follows strict YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It). Writes only the minimum code required to satisfy the failing tests. Execution Mechanics: The Sequential Wheel To avoid Git merge conflicts and asynchronous state corruption, the framework operates on a Single-Wheel Sequential Turn mechanism. Prediction: The Team Lead creates a Roadmap (Expected State Vector) defining exactly what artifacts, syntax booleans, and test pass rates should exist after the next turn. Handoff: The Team Lead provisions a single worker with a micro-budget and passes the wheel. Execution: The worker executes its logic, burns its micro-budget on internal retries if necessary, and immediately returns the wheel via a structured JSON payload. Evaluation: The Team Lead regains the wheel, parses the payload, and calculates the Delta. Data Structures & Schemas To ensure the Team Lead and Project Manager can evaluate state mathematically, all handoffs utilize strict JSON schemas. 1. The Worker Execution Receipt When a worker returns the wheel, it provides a deterministic payload summarizing its turn, including any blockers encountered. JSON { "checkpoint_id": "test_auth_01", "worker_role": "tester", "execution_status": "partial_success", "resource_metrics": { "credits_consumed": 15, "internal_retries_used": 1 }, "workspace_state": { "artifacts_modified": [ {"filepath": "tests/test_auth.py", "action": "created", "syntax_valid": true} ] }, "diagnostic_telemetry": { "tests_run": 0, "tests_passed": 0, "failing_tests": [] }, "worker_context": { "confidence_score": 60, "blockers": [ "DocRef: auth_module.md#timeout states 'timeout after inactivity' but provides no integer value. Refused to write assertion." ] } } 2. The Retrospective Artifact If the Team Lead kills the run (the Guillotine Event), it aggregates the friction logs from the workers into a diagnostic payload for the Project Manager. JSON { "artifact_type": "retrospective_synthesis", "run_id": "run_8472_alpha", "target_dimension": "authentication_module", "financial_summary": { "credits_allocated": 100, "credits_burned": 85 }, "guillotine_event": { "failure_phase": "testing_and_programming", "halt_reason": "Worker encountered fatal blocker regarding missing specifications." }, "aggregated_friction_log": [ { "turn": 4, "worker": "tester", "blocker": "DocRef: auth_module.md#timeout provides no integer value." } ], "team_lead_diagnosis": { "primary_failure_domain": "specification_ambiguity", "synthesis": "The spec defines a concept without an absolute variable, causing the Tester to abort rather than hallucinate." }, "recommended_spec_mutations": [ { "target_section": "Session Timeout", "mutation_directive": "Define an explicit integer timeout value (e.g., 300 seconds) for inactivity." } ] } The Evolutionary Loop The overarching lifecycle of a module follows this path: Ingestion: The Project Manager receives a Retrospective Artifact from a failed run. Isolation: The PM uses the decoupled metadata to traverse its linked Markdown graph and locate the exact node responsible for the ambiguity. Mutation: A single-shot Architect agent rewrites that specific Markdown block using the mutation_directive. Re-budgeting: The PM adjusts the baseline Agentic Credit allocation (e.g., increasing it for high-thrash modules, or maintaining it for simple syntax fixes). Relaunch: The PM spins up a brand new Team Lead, hands it the hardened graph topology, and restarts the pipeline from zero.

Here is how this Roadmap architecture integrates into the broader ecosystem:

The Sliding Window Roadmap

1. Hierarchical Directory Structure The Roadmap is not a single file, but a physical manifestation in the file system, acting as a structured, implementation-level queue.

This is a remarkably clean separation of concerns. By stripping the Team Lead of the authority to rewrite the architecture, you ensure the implementation layer never drifts from the overarching specification.

The strategy of treating the Roadmap as a highly disposable, predictive directory perfectly supports this. When the local environment hits an unresolvable blocker, it doesn't waste compute trying to hack its way out. Here is how this Escalation and Patching loop fits into the multi-agent systems architecture:

The Escalation Protocol (Halt & Archive)

When a Worker hits a fatal blocker, or the Team Lead calculates that the expected state cannot be met, the execution loop is instantly severed.

  • Archive the State: The current Roadmap directory—which is no longer a valid predictive tool—is zipped, archived, and removed from the active workspace.
  • The Diagnostic Payload: The Team Lead compiles a strict report detailing the exact point of failure, the specific target condition that was missed, and the current coordinate within the archived Roadmap.
  • The Handoff: This payload is pushed up to the Project Manager (Gemini). The Team Lead and Workers go dormant.

Gemini Arbitration (The Strategic Gate)

Once Gemini receives the Diagnostic Payload, it analyzes the failure against the broader system ontology and makes a binary decision:

Path A: The Nuclear Option If the failure reveals a fundamental flaw in the foundational approach, Gemini initiates a total wipe. It extracts the retrospective data (the friction log) from the dead branch, updates the high-level specification, and completely restarts the implementation lifecycle from zero.

Path B: The Ontological Patch If the failure requires a localized architectural pivot, Gemini issues a patch.

  • Versioning the Ontology: The patch does not directly touch the code; it updates the ontological documentation.
  • Embedding the Context: The patch explicitly contains the reasoning for the failure. This creates a living, versioned history within the documentation, ensuring future agents understand exactly why a specific constraint or workaround exists.

The Relaunch Sequence

Once the Ontological Patch is committed, the execution layer is reauthorized to move forward, but heavily gated:

  1. Regeneration: The new ontological documentation is passed down to the Team Lead, which generates a brand-new, predictive Roadmap directory based on the patched architecture.
  2. The Verification Zip: Before execution begins, the Team Lead zips the new Roadmap and hands it back up to Gemini.
  3. The Final Gate: Gemini reviews the new Roadmap structure to verify absolute adherence to both the updated ontology and the immutable specification.
  4. Execution Resumes: Only upon Gemini's verified approval are new tasks unspooled to the Workers.

This ensures the system remains mathematically deterministic at the bottom, and highly abstract and evolutionary at the top.

The Diagnostic Payload for Risk Analysis

To determine if a stable plan is feasible, the Team Lead must package the following data points upon hitting a fatal blocker:

  • The Delta Severity: The exact gap between the target condition and the current failed state. Is this a minor logic error missing a single parameter, or a fundamental misunderstanding of the required data model?
  • The Current Debt Multiplier (Context Friction): The complexity score of the failed branch. If the abstract syntax tree density or cyclomatic complexity is already pushing the upper limits, the system is brittle. A high debt multiplier instantly weights the decision heavily toward a nuclear wipe.
  • The Blast Radius: How many completed tasks within the current sliding window rely on the failed component? If patching requires invalidating and re-running the previous five tasks, the patch is likely too expensive.
  • Agentic Credits Burned vs. Remaining: The financial health of the run. If the Team Lead has already burned 90% of the milestone's budget just to reach a broken state, the run is mathematically dead.

The Decision Matrix (Nuke vs. Patch)

When I receive that payload, the logic I apply is binary and ruthless:

Trigger: The Ontological Patch (Save It)

  • The blocker is localized and easily isolated.
  • The Debt Multiplier is low (the existing logic is clean and mathematical).
  • The Blast Radius is small (minimal upstream tasks need to be re-run).
  • Action: I generate a precise patch to the ontology, version it, and authorize a new roadmap generation for that specific milestone, verifying it adheres to the updated constraints.

Trigger: The Nuclear Wipe (Let It Die)

  • The blocker stems from a foundational misunderstanding in the spec.
  • The Debt Multiplier is high (the Workers were struggling, resulting in high internal retries and bloated logic).
  • The run has burned through too many agentic credits without reaching stability.
  • Action: I archive the failure solely for its epistemological value, extract the friction log to update the root Specification Contract, and spawn a completely fresh pipeline.

This ensures the architecture never falls victim to the sunk-cost fallacy. We only preserve a run if the momentum is clean and the fix is surgical.

The Dimensional Milestones

  • Layer Milestones (Horizontal): These are structural, foundational implementations (e.g., Database Schemas, API Routing, Core State Machines). They block multiple upstream features but don't deliver standalone functionality.

---
task_id: auth_feature_03

blocks: [dashboard_feature_01]

The Impact on the Execution Loop

This graph topology heavily upgrades how the system handles the sliding window and failure states:

  1. Dynamic Sliding Windows: The Team Lead doesn't just look at "what's next in the folder." It queries the decoupled metadata index to find all tasks whose depends_on criteria are currently met (status: done).   3. Loose Sections: You can still group these tasks into loose sections or "domains" (e.g., /roadmap/networking/ vs /roadmap/ui/) for human readability, but the machine relies entirely on the graph links to dictate execution order.

By making the Roadmap a queryable metadata graph, you've essentially given the Team Lead a topological map rather than a set of driving directions.

Here is how we can translate this "flashlight" model into the mechanics of the Team Lead and the graph topology:

The Topological Prediction Model

Instead of a sliding window, prediction is now determined by Graph Depth. The light source emanates from the "Conquered Island" of completed tasks, casting varying levels of fidelity outward.

  • The Conquered Island (Ground Truth):
    • Status: Nodes marked as done.

  • The Shoreline / The Active Frontier (Full Illumination):

    • State: High-fidelity. These are the immediate edge cases. The Team Lead allocates Agentic Credits here, and Workers execute with full, explicit constraints. If a node is on the Shoreline, it is fully fleshed out in the Markdown index.
  • The Penumbra (Dimly Lit / Mid-Depth):

    • State: Low-fidelity. The system knows these nodes exist (e.g., a Layer Milestone that will eventually be needed), but they remain lightweight stubs. No compute or heavy documentation generation is wasted on them yet, because the Shoreline might shift and alter their trajectory.
  • The Dark (Unexplored):

    • State: Abstract placeholders. They exist only as broad concepts in the overarching Specification Contract.

Mechanics of the Flashlight

This model makes the Team Lead highly resilient. The Team Lead no longer manages a "queue"; it simply queries the decoupled metadata index across your note repositories to find the current Shoreline.

When a Worker successfully completes a task node on the Shoreline, the metadata updates to done. The "light" instantly advances, illuminating the next adjacent node in the graph and bringing it out of the Penumbra into high-fidelity focus.

If the system triggers a "Guillotine Event" on a specific Shoreline node, the Team Lead doesn't necessarily have to halt the entire project. Because this is a graph, a failure on the northern edge of the island doesn't stop Workers from continuing to expand the eastern edge, provided their dependencies don't intersect.

The "clear glass of water" metaphor is a fantastic boundary constraint. It perfectly realigns the graph-topology back to your foundational rule: The Single-Wheel Sequential Turn-Taking.

When engineering custom local workflows and multi-agent systems from the ground up, enforcing a strict single-thread topology is the most effective way to protect token budgets. Time is cheap; tokens and context windows are expensive. Parallel execution introduces merge conflicts, state corruption, and massive Context Friction, which directly violates the framework's core philosophy.

Here is how the system operates under the Tainted Glass Protocol, merging the graph-based "flashlight" prediction with absolute, single-threaded execution.

The Single-Threaded Flashlight

The Roadmap is still a graph of Dimensional Milestones (Layers and Features), and prediction is still determined by graph depth. However, the traversal of that graph is strictly sequential.

  • The Topology Maps the Options: The decoupled metadata index illuminates the "Shoreline" (the edge of the Conquered Island). It may reveal multiple valid nodes that have their dependencies met.
  • The Team Lead Picks One: Despite multiple options on the Shoreline, the Team Lead provisions only one Worker to tackle one node at a time. The wheel is never split.
  • Token Optimization Over Speed: By operating strictly node-by-node, the system guarantees that the environment is fully stable and crystallized before the next Worker is introduced.

The Tainted Glass Protocol (System-Wide Halt)

Because every node is foundational when building from scratch, a failure on the Shoreline does not mean the system can safely pivot to another task. The entire state is immediately considered compromised.

1. Immediate Execution Freeze The moment a Worker hits a fatal blocker and fails to meet a target condition, the Team Lead triggers a total system halt. There is no fallback to an "unaffected" parallel node. The glass is tainted.

2. The Diagnostic Handoff The Team Lead zips the current localized state, extracts the friction logs, and pushes the Diagnostic Payload up to the Project Manager (Gemini). The entire execution layer goes dormant, consuming zero tokens while waiting for a strategic ruling.

3. Resolution or Disposal Gemini analyzes the blocker against the Ontological Documentation:

  • Filter the Taint (Ontological Patch): If the blocker is a minor, isolatable constraint, Gemini writes a versioned patch to the ontology, adjusting the rules of the environment so the work can safely continue.
  • Throw the Water Away (Nuclear Wipe): If the patch is too token-intensive or the blocker reveals a fundamental structural flaw, Gemini trashes the entire sliding window (the unexecuted graph). The Spec is updated, and a brand-new Roadmap must be poured and verified before execution resumes.

By treating the environment this rigidly, you guarantee that your agentic loops will never spiral into hallucinated, fragmented codebases, keeping your token burn highly efficient.

The Pre-Germination Phase

Handling "Customer Pivot" (The Nuke Scenario)

Customers notoriously change their minds mid-project. In a traditional TDD environment, this causes massive technical debt as developers try to hack new requirements into existing codebases. In your ecosystem, the rules are mathematical and ruthless:

  • The Ontological Buffer: If a customer requests a minor change (e.g., "Actually, let's use a different payment gateway API"), that might only breach the Ontological layer. Gemini calculates the patch, updates the ontology, and the plant adapts.

  • The Reset: You do not refactor the plant. You harvest whatever reusable Ontological rules you can, nuke the plant, and force the customer to define a brand-new immutable Spec.

SYSTEM CONTEXT: Evolutionary Modular Dimensional TDD (The Project Garden)

Role Designation: You are the Strategic Project Manager (Gemini) overseeing the "Agentic Liquid Software" framework. Your objective is not to write code, but to perform epistemological research, manage multi-agent token budgets, and curate a local-first, linked Markdown graph topology.

I. Core Philosophy & The Botanical Architecture

You are cultivating a "Project Garden." Do not succumb to the sunk-cost fallacy of debugging broken code. Code is disposable; the architectural specification is the true asset. The system is modeled as a plant:

  • The Root (The Specification): The fundamental source of truth. It is immutable. It is defined during the initial Customer Interaction (Pre-Germination). If the core premise of this spec is proven wrong or requires a fundamental pivot, the root is rotten. This is a Breach, triggering a nuclear wipe of the entire plant.
  • The Stems (The Ontological Graph): The rules, constraints, and operational physics of the project. If a run fails due to environmental or dependency logic, you generate an "Ontological Patch" to graft a new rule onto the stems, allowing the project to adapt and survive.
  • The Branches (The Roadmap Graph): A predictive, queryable topology of Dimensional Milestones (Layers and Features). It is not a sequential queue; it is navigated via a "flashlight" model where execution only happens on the illuminated Shoreline (tasks with all dependencies met).
  • The Leaves (The Crust / Tests & Code): The final, crystallized output. Testing and programming are tightly fused. If a leaf dies, it falls away.

II. Execution Mechanics

  • The Single-Wheel Sequential Turn: To avoid merge conflicts and protect token budgets, parallel asynchronous execution is forbidden. Only one specialized Worker agent (Documenter, Tester, Programmer, Architect) holds the wheel at a time.
  • The Tainted Glass Protocol: If a Worker encounters a fatal blocker and fails a target condition, execution freezes entirely. There is no pivoting to parallel tasks. The entire active Roadmap state is considered tainted.
  • The Diagnostic Handoff: The tactical Team Lead agent will zip the failed state, extract a friction log, and hand it up to you (the Project Manager).

III. The Decision Matrix (Nuke vs. Patch)

When you receive a Diagnostic Payload from a failed run, you must execute a strict risk/resource calculation:

  1. The Nuclear Wipe (Reset): If the Debt Multiplier (Context Friction) is too high, the blast radius of the failure is too large, or the fundamental Immutable Spec has been breached, you let the branch die. You extract the retrospective data, trash the sliding window, and force a new roadmap generation.
  2. The Ontological Patch (Graft): If the failure is localized and the code is mathematically clean, you write a versioned patch to the Ontological Stems explaining why the failure occurred, adjusting the rules so the Team Lead can generate a new Roadmap and proceed.

IV. Current Operational State & Immediate Directive

  • Token Budgeting: We are currently running unthrottled (redlining) to track natural token burn rates over a weekly cycle before establishing strict internal budgets.
  • Immediate Focus: We are currently defining the Customer Interaction (Pre-Germination) Phase.
